name: Event buses
summary: A router that sends each event to whoever has a rule for it.
howItWorks: Services and SaaS apps emit events to one central bus. Rules match events on their fields (source, type, even values inside the payload) and deliver them to targets such as functions, queues, workflows or other accounts. It’s pub/sub with content-based routing and filtering built in, so each consumer receives only the events it asked for.
analogy: A mailroom that reads each envelope and drops it in the right pigeonholes, following rules each department filed.
useWhen: Many event types from many sources, with routing that changes often
Reacting to cloud and SaaS events: a file landed, a payment settled
Cross-team or cross-account integration without point-to-point wiring
avoidWhen: Very high-throughput telemetry; per-event pricing and latency favor a stream
Strict ordering across all events; most buses don’t promise order, and EventBridge’s new Custom Event Bus orders only within an event group
example: Payments, orders and field alarms all publish to one bus. A rule sends `alarm` events with `severity=critical` to the on-call pager and to email, while `order` events start the fulfilment workflow.

story: The event bus descends from the integration middleware of the 1990s and 2000s. As companies tried to connect dozens of applications, the enterprise service bus (ESB) became the fashion; the first published use of the term is credited to Gartner’s Roy Schulte, in 2002. An ESB was a central hub that routed, transformed and mediated messages between systems. It cut point-to-point wiring, but it could become a single point of failure and needed heavy configuration.

The 2003 book Enterprise Integration Patterns named the building blocks, including the Message Bus and the Content-Based Router, which routes “each message to the correct recipient based on message content.” Cloud event buses kept the routing and dropped the heavy middle. AWS shipped CloudWatch Events in 2016 to route AWS’s own resource events to functions with rules, Microsoft previewed Azure Event Grid in 2017, and AWS relaunched its service as EventBridge in 2019 so SaaS companies could publish into customers’ buses.

Two trends are shaping it now: CloudEvents, a CNCF specification for describing events the same way everywhere, and buses that keep events, such as EventBridge’s Custom Event Bus of 2026, with retention, replay and ordering, which bring event buses closer to streams.

choices.choice: Route on content, not on addresses
choices.why: Producers emit events without naming a receiver, and rules match on fields such as source, type or values in the payload. Each consumer gets only what it asked for, and routing changes don’t touch producers.

choices.choice: A managed router, not a central integration server
choices.why: ESBs became single points of failure that needed heavy configuration. Cloud buses are run by the provider, scale per event and leave business logic in producers and consumers.

choices.choice: The platform publishes its own events
choices.why: Cloud providers put their resource events (a file uploaded, an instance stopped) on the bus, so reacting to infrastructure needs no polling. Event Grid launched with Blob Storage and resource group events.
Every publisher describing events differently made each integration custom. CloudEvents defines common metadata so tools and buses can handle any event the same way.
